newsitem.title: UK: Strike grounds hundreds of BA flights.
newsitem.headline: Strike grounds hundreds of BA flights.

text.p: Striking cabin crew forced British Airways to cancel half its flights out of London on Wednesday, leaving more than 25,000 passengers stranded.

The airline's Heathrow Airport hub bore the brunt of the disruption from the three-day strike, with less than one in three flights able to go ahead. BA said, worldwide, 70 to 80 percent of flights would go ahead, after a company spokeswoman earlier said just 20 percent of its flights would take off.
London's stock market shrugged off worries about the strike and the company's shares rose on hopes that a settlement for the dispute was within reach.
But the airline said newspaper reports that a breakthrough could be made through the appointment of an independent arbiter were "inaccurate".

Members of the Transport and General Workers' Union (T&G) began the strike at 0500 GMT in the face of warnings by management that strikers would lose perks and face a lockout unless they promised to work normally in the future.
But the union pledged to stand firm.
"Despite all the threats, I can report that the dispute is solid," general secretary Bill Morris told the union's conference in Brighton.
He said the union remained prepared to negotiate.

"We are committed to negotiating and we are ready to talk, but we are not going to be bullied," Morris said. "We will discuss our future relationship with BA, but we never ever abandon our members in the face of industrial dictatorship."
Pickets carrying banners gathered in the early morning sun near BA's headquarters at Heathrow, while usually frenetic Terminal One was eerily quiet.
Pickets were also stationed outside other British airports and some were even flown to New York to try to win support from workers there.
BA had hoped to save 42 million pounds ($70.7 million) from its cabin crew operations. The unions oppose the cuts and unless a solution is found, are threatening further 72-hour strikes.
BA spokeswoman Terri Urquart said the airline was "very hopeful" of progress in resolving the dispute, but added: "As yet, no sign of any movement."
British travel agents have been flooded with calls from customers trying to find alternative flights on rival airlines.
BA said its contingency plan, aimed at keeping as many of its flights running as possible, was swinging into action but it admitted thousands of passengers may still be grounded.
Industry analysts said the impact would be severe.

"The damage will be huge," said Chris Avery, European airlines analyst at Paribas in London. "The damage to the airline's reputation amongst premium traffic is going to be very difficult to recover. This is a very competitive industry where there are plenty of alternatives."
